title: Connection pooling, the thing that quietly kills serverless apps
story:
A database connection is expensive twice over, and the two costs are unrelated, which is why the failure it produces is so confusing.

The first cost is establishing one. The second is holding one, and that cost is architectural. The documentation describes the arrangement as a process per user client-server model in which every client process connects to exactly one backend process: because it is not known ahead of time how many connections will be made, a supervisor process called the postmaster listens on a port and spawns a new backend process every time a connection is requested. A connection is not a socket and a bit of bookkeeping. It is an operating system process with its own memory, scheduled by the kernel, communicating with its peers through semaphores and shared memory.

So there is a hard limit, and it is a configured one. The max_connections parameter determines the maximum number of concurrent connections, the default is typically 100 but might be less if kernel settings will not support it, it can only be set at server start, and the server sizes certain resources based directly on its value — so increasing it leads to higher allocation of those resources, including shared memory. That last clause is why raising the number is not free and not a fix.

A pool is the response: keep a small set of established connections, lend them out, take them back. Establishment is paid once per connection instead of once per request, and the number held is bounded by the pool rather than by traffic.

And here is the part that catches people, because the arithmetic is invisible until it is not. A pool is per process. The connections your database sees is the pool size multiplied by the number of processes holding pools. Eight workers with a pool of ten across three replicas is two hundred and forty connections from one deployment, and the background worker deployment with the same defaults is another. In a long-running deployment that product is fixed and can be reasoned about. In a runtime that creates a process per request, it is not bounded at all — three hundred concurrent invocations are three hundred pools, each thinking it is being modest.

Which produces the signature failure: the database refuses connections while its processor sits nearly idle. The error is a count, not a measure of load, and every instinct that treats it as overload sends you the wrong way. The structural answer is a pooler in front that multiplexes many client connections onto a few server ones — and it works because most clients are not executing anything at any given moment.

problem.name: Connection scarcity
problem.shape: Each connection to the database is an operating system process, and the number of them is capped well below the number of things that want one.
tell: connection errors appear while database processor usage is low
the number of application instances varies with traffic
each request opens its own connection
raising the connection limit was the last fix applied
problem.move: Count the connections your deployment can produce — pool size times processes, including every deployment and burst setting — before tuning anything. Where processes are long-running, shrink the per-process pool. Where a process is created per request, a client-side pool cannot bound anything and you need a pooler in front that multiplexes many clients onto few server connections.
problem.invariant: Every client connection is a separate backend process spawned by a supervisor, so connections consume memory and scheduling whether or not they are executing anything, and their maximum is fixed at server start.
problem.breaks: The limit is a count and not a measure of load, so it can be exhausted by idle connections while the server does almost no work — and the two obvious responses both fail. Raising the limit allocates more resources including shared memory, and enlarging the pool increases the very number that is exhausting it.

cost.time: a checkout from the pool per unit of work, against the cost of establishing a connection which includes forking, authenticating and negotiating encryption
cost.space: memory per held connection whether busy or idle, on the database rather than in your application
cost.beats: a connection per request, which pays establishment every time and bounds nothing, and one shared connection, which serialises everything behind it

worked.problem: Your database is refusing connections while its processor sits nearly idle. What is happening?
worked.reasoning:
You have exhausted a count, not a capacity — and those are different resources that happen to produce one error message.

The architecture is the reason. Every client process connects to exactly one backend process, and because it is not known in advance how many connections will be made, a supervisor process spawns a new backend every time one is requested. So a connection is an operating system process with its own memory, scheduled by the kernel. Holding one costs resources even when it is doing nothing at all, which is precisely how you arrive at exhaustion with an idle processor.

The ceiling is configured rather than emergent: the parameter determining the maximum number of concurrent connections defaults to around a hundred, may be lower if kernel settings will not support it, and can only be changed at server start. So this failure has a fixed threshold that traffic can cross without the workload getting any heavier.

The next step is arithmetic rather than investigation. Connections equals pool size times the number of processes holding pools, summed over every deployment. Eight workers with a pool of ten across three replicas is two hundred and forty from one service before the background workers are counted, and application pools usually have burst settings above their nominal size, so the ceiling is what matters rather than the steady state. A rolling deployment briefly doubles it while old and new replicas coexist.

That arithmetic is why a runtime creating a process per request is a different problem in kind rather than degree. Each concurrent invocation is a fresh process with a fresh pool, so three hundred concurrent requests are three hundred pools, each individually modest. No client-side configuration bounds the product because the multiplicand is set by traffic.

So the responses, in order. First count, using the server's own view of who is connected, because the answer is usually one deployment nobody was thinking about. Then, if processes are fixed in number, shrink the per-process pool — that often removes the error without new infrastructure. If processes are created per request, add a pooler in front that multiplexes many client connections onto a few server ones, which works because most clients are not executing anything at any instant.

And the two instincts to resist. Raising the limit allocates more resources including shared memory and gives you more processes competing, which usually performs worse than fewer pooled ones. Enlarging the pool increases the very number that is exhausting you. I would also check whether something downstream got slower, because when queries take longer, connections are held longer and pile up — in that case the exhaustion is the symptom and the slow query is the disease.

problem.practice: Compute your worst-case connection count on paper: every deployment, times its process count, times its pool ceiling including burst, and add a rolling deployment's overlap. Compare it to the server's configured maximum. Then ask the server who is actually connected and see which deployment you forgot.

beats.broke: Opening a connection is expensive and holding one is expensive for a different reason, so a system that opens one per unit of work pays both costs on every request.
beats.fix: Keep a small set of established connections and lend them out, so establishment is paid once per connection rather than once per request and the number held is bounded by the pool rather than by traffic.
beats.cost: The pool is per process, so the total held is pool size times however many processes exist — fixed in a long-running deployment and unbounded in one that creates a process per request.

interview.q: Your database is refusing connections while its processor sits nearly idle. What is happening?
interview.trap: Reading it as overload and raising the limit or enlarging the pool. It is a count rather than a measure of load — raising the limit allocates more shared memory and adds competing processes, and enlarging the pool increases the number that is exhausting you.
interview.answer:
You have exhausted a count rather than a capacity, and those are different resources that produce one error message.

The architecture explains it. Every client process connects to exactly one backend process, and because the number of connections is not known in advance, a supervisor spawns a new backend each time one is requested. A connection is therefore an operating system process with its own memory, scheduled by the kernel — so holding one costs resources while doing nothing, which is exactly how you exhaust the limit with an idle processor.

The ceiling is configured rather than emergent: the parameter defaults to around a hundred, may be lower if kernel settings will not support it, and can only be changed at server start. So the threshold is fixed and traffic can cross it without the workload getting heavier.

The next step is arithmetic. Connections equals pool size times processes holding pools, summed across every deployment — eight workers with a pool of ten across three replicas is two hundred and forty before background workers, pools usually have burst settings above nominal so the ceiling matters rather than the steady state, and a rolling deployment briefly doubles it.

That arithmetic is why process-per-request runtimes are a different problem in kind: each concurrent invocation is a fresh process with a fresh pool, so three hundred concurrent requests are three hundred modest pools, and no client-side configuration bounds the product because the multiplicand is traffic.

So: count first, using the server's view of who is connected, since the answer is usually a deployment nobody was thinking about. If processes are fixed, shrink the per-process pool, which often removes the error without new infrastructure. If processes are per request, put a pooler in front that multiplexes many clients onto few server connections — which works because most clients are not executing anything at any instant.

I would also check whether something downstream got slower, since longer queries mean connections held longer and piling up — in which case exhaustion is the symptom and the slow query is the disease.
